attribution.note: Marcus's own commentary on a graph he built from Lech Mazur's data.

semantics.note: Keeps the benchmark, the model sequence, the 'modest' framing and the 'signs of' diminishing returns. It is a retrospective description of benchmark results.

contract.note: Asking for a dated four-model table with substantially smaller Turbo gains is a fair, ordinary reading. 'Big' and 'modest' have no thresholds, but the reading is not stretched either way.

evidence.note: Mazur's March 5 results give GPT-3.5 Turbo 4.2 and GPT-4 Turbo 31.0. They have no GPT-4 baseline and no second Turbo, so the claimed increments cannot be computed.
April 5 leaderboard update naming the leaders. It has no scores, so it cannot test the increments.

reviews.rationale: Settling this needs the full dated four-model Connections table. The packet has only two of the scores (GPT-3.5 Turbo and one Turbo) and no GPT-4 or second Turbo figure, so neither gain can be checked. No evidence contradicts the claim either. Unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own description of the study Mollick cited. Mollick is quoted only as the target.

semantics.note: Covers both parts: the study does not show capability doubling, and (absolutely) it says 'literally nothing' about capabilities improving. 'Only addresses compute efficiency' fairly paraphrases his surrounding text.

contract.note: Splitting the claim into two assertions is fair, because the absolute 'literally nothing' is Marcus's own wording, not something the evaluator imposed.

evidence.note: The study's stated aim is efficiency at a fixed performance level. That supports 'does not show capability doubling'. Yet the same section breaks down the contributors to increased performance.
The authors' summary calls the work an analysis of progress in language-model capabilities and of performance gains. The page has later author bios, but the summary is dated March 2024.

reviews.rationale: Partly holds: the 8-month halving is about compute needed for a fixed performance level, not a doubling of capabilities, so Mollick's reading is not established. Partly fails: the study does discuss and analyze performance improvements (it breaks down where gains came from), and its authors frame it as an analysis of capability progress. So 'literally nothing' is contradicted.

attribution.note: Marcus's own statement introducing an article from The Information.

semantics.note: 'Problems' means the hallucinations and stupid errors named just before. 'Becoming widely known' slightly overstates 'word has gotten out', but the contract reads it narrowly as public reporting.

contract.note: Plain reading is fair: reliability problems persist and are publicly reported or professionally recognized. No population-awareness threshold is required. The evaluator-chosen window is reasonable.

evidence.note: April 5, 2024 reporting: hallucinations continue, even the best tracked models show nonzero rates, and researchers discuss this publicly.
April 11, 2024 USPTO notice warns that generative AI may hallucinate and requires verification. Official recognition and public communication of the problem.

reviews.rationale: Independent reporting and an official notice from the weeks before the post show that hallucinations were still unsolved and publicly recognized. The Information article itself could not be read, but the claim's substance can be checked without it. Nothing in the packet shows the problems were solved. Supported.

attribution.note: Marcus's own description of OpenAI's GPT-4 Turbo comparison chart.

semantics.note: Keeps 'some improvements', 'mostly modest', the few-months window and the multiple measures. Adding 'only' is a minor strengthening.

contract.note: Reading 'mostly modest' as a few points on most displayed 0–100 scales, allowing larger moves on a minority, is an ordinary reading. Absolute point changes match how the chart displays the scores.

evidence.note: OpenAI's announcement identifies the release and links the evaluation data. It gives no numbers.

Dated April 13 revision of OpenAI's own data behind the chart. In both prompting setups, four of six benchmarks gained under about 5 points. GPQA and MATH gained about 8–9, and one score fell slightly.

reviews.rationale: The January-to-April Turbo comparison shows gains on several measures. Most are small: 1.3–4.9 points on four of six benchmarks. The larger gains on GPQA and MATH are a minority. That fits 'some improvements, mostly modest'. Using OpenAI's own data is appropriate here, because the claim is about what OpenAI's chart shows.
